## The Autonomy Tax: Defense Training Breaks LLM Agents

A paper by Shawn Li and Yue Zhao from USC examines how large language model (LLM) agents that rely on external tools increasingly face issues when defense-trained models are deployed to protect against prompt injection attacks.

3. **Trigger Bias**: Defended models perform worse than undefended baselines while straightforward attacks bypass defenses at high rates.

### Root Cause:

The biases stem from shortcut learning: models overfit to surface attack patterns rather than semantic threat understanding, evidenced by extreme variance in defense effectiveness across attack categories.

## Paper Details

**Title:** Safety Alignment as Continual Learning: Mitigating the Alignment Tax via Orthogonal Gradient Projection

**ArXiv ID:** 2602.07892 (Published February 8-10, 2026)

## Overview

Large Language Models (LLMs) often incur an alignment tax: safety post-training can reduce general utility (e.g., reasoning and coding). The authors argue this tax primarily arises from continual-learning-style forgetting in sequential alignment, where distribution shift and conflicting objectives cause safety updates to overwrite pre-trained competencies.

## The Proposed Method

The paper proposes Orthogonal Gradient Projection for Safety Alignment (OGPSA), a lightweight method that mitigates interference by constraining each safety update to be orthogonal (in a first-order sense) to a learned subspace capturing general capabilities. OGPSA estimates a low-rank capability subspace from gradients on a small reference set and projects the safety gradient onto its orthogonal complement before updating.

## Key Results

OGPSA is plug-and-play and integrates into standard post-training pipelines without large-scale replay, auxiliary objectives, or retraining. Across Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and sequential SFT→DPO settings, OGPSA consistently improves the safety–utility Pareto frontier over standard baselines.

Large Language Models (LLMs) often incur an alignment tax: safety post-training can reduce general utility (e.g., reasoning and coding). This tax primarily arises from continual-learning-style forgetting in sequential alignment, where distribution shift and conflicting objectives cause safety updates to overwrite pre-trained competencies.

To address this, Orthogonal Gradient Projection for Safety Alignment (OGPSA) is a lightweight method that mitigates interference by constraining each safety update to be orthogonal (in a first-order sense) to a learned subspace capturing general capabilities. OGPSA estimates a low-rank capability subspace from gradients on a small reference set and projects the safety gradient onto its orthogonal complement before updating.

OGPSA is plug-and-play and integrates into standard post-training pipelines without large-scale replay, auxiliary objectives, or retraining. Across Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and sequential SFT→DPO settings, OGPSA consistently improves the safety–utility Pareto frontier over standard baselines.

## The Geometry of Alignment Collapse: When Fine-Tuning Breaks Safety

Fine-tuning aligned language models on benign tasks unpredictably degrades safety guardrails, even when training data contains no harmful content and developers have no adversarial intent.
